articles.title: Twins, Sonny Gray agree to deal reportedly for 2 years and worth $55 million with an opt-out
articles.summary: Gray returns to Minnesota, where he spent the 2022 and 2023 seasons.
articles.body:
The Minnesota Twins and starting pitcher Sonny Gray have agreed to a deal.

The team confirmed the signing Wednesday on social media, and ESPN's Jeff Passan reported that the deal is a two-year, $55 million contract with an opt-out after the first year.

Gray returns to Minnesota, where he spent the 2022 and 2023 seasons. In his previous stint with the Twins, Gray started 56 games over two seasons, tallying a 16-13 record and a 2.90 ERA.

The 37-year-old spent last season with the Boston Red Sox where he made 29 starts and finished with a career-high 18 wins. Gray went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and struck out 149 batters in 169 innings.

His wins and ERA were Boston's best last season. Gray's 18 wins were tied with Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Cristopher Sánchez and Arizona Diamondbacks southpaw Eduardo Rodríguez for most in MLB last season. The veteran right-hander's 2.72 ERA was the eighth-best in all of baseball.

Minnesota has plenty of time to make more moves, but for now Gray looks to bolster a 2027 rotation consisting of Joe Ryan, Pablo López, Dean Kremer and Taj Bradley. López missed all of last season due to Tommy John surgery, but is expected to be ready toward the start of next season, pending a lockout.

This is the Twins' second deal this offseason. Minnesota extended a qualifying offer to catcher Ryan Jeffers. The catcher accepted it and will earn $23.15 million next season with the Twins.

articles.title: New Tarik Skubal Rumors Uncover Mets' 'All-In' Approach Amid Dodgers Buzz in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The New York Mets are pushing all of their chips to Tarik Skubal's side of the table.
articles.body:
The New York Mets are pushing all of their chips to Tarik Skubal's side of the table.

According to Jon Heyman of the New York Post , "the Mets seem even more determined to sign superstar free-agent left-hander Skubal after meeting with the two-time Cy Young winner Monday in Orange County, California. Mets people came away uber impressed with MLB's top free agent. Word going around is that the Mets' deep-pocketed owner Steve Cohen is expected to be 'all in' for Skubal."

Heyman added that the Los Angeles Dodgers, San Diego Padres and Toronto Blue Jays remain in the hunt for Skubal.

It has been no secret, however, that the Mets are trying to land the ace pitcher:

Skubal, 29, seems likely to sign a deal that will set a new record for pitchers, perhaps one in the $300-400 million range. That will naturally take some teams out of the running, though the Mets have never shied away from such deals.

Juan Soto, for instance, signed a 15-year, $750 million deal with the team in Dec. 2024, the most total money for a contract in MLB history (Shohei Ohtani's 10-year, $500 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers is the highest average annual salary, at $50 million, in the history of the sport).

Soto has largely lived up to that deal, sans some injury issues this past season. The bigger issue has been the team's inability to construct a true contender around him.

Getting Skubal would help. The two-time AL Cy Young winner finished 12-7 last season between the Detroit Tigers and the Dodgers with a 2.72 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings. It is a testament to Skubal's greatness that his 2026 performance was a bit of a down year (though he did miss about five weeks of the season due to loose bodies in his pitching elbow).

He's the top free agent on the market, without question, and would be a major addition for whichever team lands him (even if there are uncertainties about when he'll actually pitch next, given the looming labor dispute). Certainly the Mets aren't being shy about their interest.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors Reveal Former AL Manager of the Year Eyed for Boone's Staff After Ausmus Exit
articles.summary: The New York Yankees are targeting former Baltimore Orioles manager Brandon Hyde for the team's bench coach vacancy, according to Joel Sherman of the New York Post.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees are targeting former Baltimore Orioles manager Brandon Hyde for the team's bench coach vacancy, according to Joel Sherman of the New York Post .

"Former Orioles manager Brandon Hyde has been in conversation with the Yankees about their bench coach job and is expected to get a more formal interview in the coming days, three sources told The Post ," Sherman reported Wednesday.

Brad Ausmus previously served as New York's bench coach under Aaron Boone from 2024-26 before he was hired as the Houston Astros' new manager on Nov. 11.

As for Hyde, he operated as Baltimore's manager from 2019-25.

He compiled a record of 421-492 during his tenure with the Orioles, helping them make two playoff appearances. This included a 2023 season in which Baltimore went 101-61, as Hyde earned American League Manager of the Year honors.

While the Orioles went 0-5 in the postseason throughout his time with the club, his experience still makes him an intriguing option for New York.

The Yankees have won at least 93 games in each of the past two years, but have suffered ALDS exits in both seasons.

While it's worth noting that New York was without three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge during its latest playoff run due to a rib injury , the Bronx Bombers are still attempting to take a step forward in 2027.

articles.title: Maikel Garcia trade: This blockbuster deal looks like a win-win for Mariners and Royals
articles.summary: For two AL clubs coming off dismally disappointing seasons, this is a fairly stunning shake-up, a bold trade underscoring each front office's priorities in r...
articles.body:
To the surprise of absolutely no one, the first blockbuster trade of the MLB offseason went down Wednesday courtesy of the swap-happy Seattle Mariners.

It was no secret that the Mariners were willing to part with some of their enviable starting pitching depth in order to upgrade their position player group, and they found an intriguing partner in the Kansas City Royals. The deal is headlined by 26-year-old Gold Glove third baseman Maikel Garcia, shipped to Seattle along with right-handed pitchers James McArthur and L.P. Langevin in exchange for three major-league arms: right-handed starters Bryce Miller and Logan Evans, plus lefty reliever Jose A. Ferrer.

For two American League clubs coming off dismally disappointing seasons, this is a fairly stunning shake-up, a bold trade underscoring each front office's priorities in regards to improving their respective rosters this winter.

It was less than a year ago when Garcia signed a long-term extension with the Royals that appeared to lock him into the hot corner alongside shortstop and franchise pillar Bobby Witt Jr. for the foreseeable future. That deal guaranteed Garcia $57.5 million with escalators for more, running through the 2030 season with a $21 million club option for 2031. It was the culmination of Garcia's astonishing decade-long development, from signing with Kansas City in 2016 as a skinny teenager out of Venezuela to becoming one of the most impactful infielders in the majors.

While Garcia's bloodlines put him on the radar early in his career — Ronald Acuña Jr. and Alcides Escobar are among several of Maikel's big-league cousins — his progression as a prospect was a slow burn. He methodically climbed the Royals' system and debuted as a 22-year-old in 2022, but he was primarily a speed-and-defense bottom-of-the-order hitter (77 wRC+) across his first two major-league seasons despite promising underlying metrics suggesting untapped potential at the plate.

Then in 2025, Garcia enjoyed a huge breakout with the bat, better translating his exceptional below-the-surface skills (plus plate discipline, strong hard-hit rates) into actual production (16 home runs, 120 wRC+). In tandem with his outstanding defense and fantastic baserunning, Garcia was suddenly an all-around force. He made his first All-Star appearance and finished with 5.6 fWAR, which ranked 14th among all major-league position players. That huge step forward motivated Kansas City to commit to Garcia with a sizable extension, while Garcia was willing to forgo free agency by a few years in order to secure an enormous guaranteed sum as a 25-year-old.

Before the 2026 season had even begun, Garcia further validated his upward trajectory by starring for Team Venezuela in the World Baseball Classic. He hit .385/.393/.577 across seven games and was named tournament MVP as Venezuela claimed its first WBC title with a riveting triumph in the finals over Team USA. Garcia then returned to the Royals and started the regular season strongly, hitting .285/.353/.437 over his first 39 games. But a muscle strain in his left hand began to bother Garcia shortly thereafter, and his production plummeted until he was eventually placed on the injured list in late June. That nagging hand ailment plus a left hamstring strain in August limited Garcia to 13 more games the rest of the way as the Royals tumbled down the standings and totally off the radar in the second half.

By the end of the year, Garcia had played in just 82 games and posted a .715 OPS with three home runs, an underwhelming encore to his breakout 2025 and one of several things that went wrong for the last-place Royals. But much higher on the list of reasons behind Kansas City's wayward campaign was its abysmal pitching staff that ranked 27th in ERA and 29th in fWAR. A poor bullpen was the biggest culprit behind those rankings, but the rotation sorely underperformed as well outside of Michael Wacha.

It was clear that improving on the mound would be a priority for Kansas City this offseason, but it was unclear how the Royals could achieve such gains. No one was expecting a run at Tarik Skubal, but would they splurge (by their standards, anyway) on a free-agent pitcher or two? Could they gather enough from their shallow farm system to add a proven pitcher via trade?

Perhaps these avenues could still be explored. But first, general manager J.J. Picollo has decided to trade a significant major-league piece in Garcia in order to address this glaring need — and found a pitching-rich trade partner in the Mariners who were eager to collaborate.

What's the upside for Mariners in this Garcia gamble?

As the Mariners have drafted and developed an entire homegrown starting rotation over the past half-decade, there has been widespread speculation league-wide regarding their willingness to part with any of that depth in order to upgrade other parts of their roster. Those whispers grew quite loud this summer at the trade deadline as Seattle tried to get its season back on track, but the Mariners ended up only subtracting veteran Luis Castillo from the rotation in a money-motivated trade with the Chicago White Sox that included getting reliever Seranthony Domínguez, outfielder Nolan Jones and catching prospect Boston Smith. Castillo's contract and poor performance made him a different kind of trade chip rather than an especially valuable piece used to acquire a meaningful major-league upgrade.

And so, by the time the Mariners made it to the end of their miserably disappointing campaign, questions again resurfaced about whether Seattle would finally make a major deal involving their wealth of starting pitching. At the GM Meetings in Las Vegas last week, president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto addressed that possibility head-on.

"We're eight deep, in my mind, on the pitching side," Dipoto said. That octet consisted of three buckets of pitchers. The first is the most proven trio of Logan Gilbert, George Kirby and Bryan Woo, each of whom has been an All-Star in recent years. The second is another trio of right-handers — Miller, Emerson Hancock and Evans — who have varied wildly in effectiveness and availability but project as dependable rotation options in 2027. Rounding out the implied group of eight was the pair of top-tier pitching prospects in 22-year-old left-hander Kade Anderson and 20-year-old Ryan Sloan, the former of whom made his major-league debut last August.

"We've always been open to listening," Dipoto said. "We have sometimes been the protagonist in engaging. Obviously, we've not gotten to the point outside of Luis Castillo this summer where we've done something. It'll take a lot. Excuse me. It'll take a lot for us to move one. And I think in general our preference would be to keep all your pitchers — you're gonna need them.

"But if it can allow us access to a hitter we otherwise wouldn't be able to access through prospect packages, position-player deals, or free agency — then we have to be open."

That sentiment set the stage for the kind of deal that came together Wednesday, as Garcia perfectly fits the description of a player worthy of finally cashing in these starting pitching chips.

With Randy Arozarena expected to depart in free agency, the Mariners were hoping to make an impactful addition to the position player group in some form, but that didn't necessarily mean bringing in another big bat of a similar ilk. Dipoto has made it crystal clear that improving Seattle's "atrocious" defense was a priority this offseason, and while Garcia's offensive track record is more mixed — and how his bat will translate to hitter-unfriendly T-Mobile Park remains to be seen — his terrific glove is undisputed. That made him an especially ideal target. He could slot in seamlessly at third base, or cover shortstop depending on how Seattle views the next steps for 21-year-old Colt Emerson, the talented infielder who endured a bumpy first taste of the majors in 2026. The versatile veteran Brendan Donovan — limited to just 39 games because of various injuries in his first season as a Mariner — could also cover third base depending on Emerson's readiness, but now projects to mostly handle left field in Arozarena's absence.

Even an average version of Garcia could be a real difference-maker for Seattle on both sides of the ball. His plus contact skills and baserunning brings some much-needed balance to a lineup that badly lacks that style of play, and his elite glovework should aid in the Mariners' run-prevention efforts. And if Garcia can flush his injury-marred 2026 and restore his full-fledged All-Star form, the Mariners may have landed a true foundational piece, and one under contract for the long haul. Add in an intriguing injury bounceback candidate for the bullpen in McArthur — who quietly logged 18 saves for the Royals in 2024 — and a swing-and-miss machine in the Québécois right-hander Langevin (LAWN-juh-van), and the Mariners may have gotten more than just an everyday infielder.

How Kansas City plans to replace a mainstay like Garcia is unknown. But the Royals evidently viewed pitching as their biggest problem and have added three potential solutions to a staff that unquestionably needed a whole lot more help than the lineup. The post-Garcia Royals still feature a strong offensive core with Witt, Jac Caglianone and Carter Jensen, but adding arms was paramount if the Royals want to reenter the mix as a contender in the AL Central.

Miller is the de facto headliner heading to Kansas City on the basis of his peak performance in the majors — a 2.94 ERA across 180 1/3 innings in 2024 — but his performance and health have fluctuated to an extreme degree over the past two seasons. Though he has not undergone surgery, Miller has dealt with bone spurs in his right elbow dating back to 2025, when he was quite poor during the regular season (5.68 ERA) before showing surprisingly well across three postseason outings. The start of his 2026 campaign was then delayed by an oblique strain. He was spectacular once he rejoined the rotation, posting a 1.71 ERA in 52 2/3 innings through his first nine outings. The rest of the season, however, was a disaster: Seattle lost 12 of his final 13 outings as Miller's ERA soared to 6.14 and nearly all of his pitches were pummeled.

His durability remains a major question mark, but Miller has time to get right as a possible anchor in the Royals' rotation (he's under contract through 2029). Like new rotation mate Seth Lugo, Miller has an absurdly deep arsenal, having showcased nine different pitch types since he debuted in the majors with his four-seamer, splitter and slider leading the way. On top of his intriguing profile as a pitcher, the proud Texan was a beloved personality in Seattle's clubhouse and should make fast friends with his new organization, and could become a fan favorite in a hurry in Kansas City if he can become a staple on the Royals' starting staff.

Evans is more of a mystery box, having made 15 starts as a rookie with Seattle in 2025 before suffering an elbow injury necessitating Tommy John surgery that put him on the shelf for all of 2026. The 25-year-old right-hander was the quintessential development story within Seattle's renowned pitching apparatus, an unheralded 12th-round pick with a 6.78 career ERA in college who surged to the big leagues in just two years. Like Miller, Evans, too, has a diverse repertoire — he threw six different pitches at least 10% of the time as a rookie — but below-average fastball velocity could limit his overall ceiling to more of an inning-eating back-end arm. If he can find another tick or two of velocity post-surgery, there could be more upside here.

Ferrer finalizes the three-pitcher package, traded for the second straight offseason after arriving in Seattle from Washington last December in a one-for-one swap for catching prospect Harry Ford. Ferrer is tremendous at coaxing ground-ball contact, which was unfortunately far too often penalized by the Mariners' lackluster defense behind him. Seattle was unable to generate more whiffs from the hard-throwing lefty — his strikeout rate actually went down from where it was with the Nationals — but it's not difficult to understand why Ferrer would still appeal to a team in dire need of bullpen help. He's under contract through 2029, throws quite hard for a southpaw (98 mph average fastball) and has proven admirably durable over the past two years, tied for fourth in the majors in appearances over that span with 145.

He might not be closer material, but Ferrer's arrival immediately improves Kansas City's most obvious weak spot, while inviting further questions about how Seattle plans to reinforce its own shaky relief corps this winter.

articles.title: Kingston pitcher commits to one of the country's top baseball programs
articles.summary: Kingston junior Vaka Tameilau developed into a top college pitching prospect, and a powerhouse SEC program has taken note.
articles.body:
By the time former Bainbridge High School baseball star JR Ritchie finished the summer baseball season prior to his junior year, the right-handed pitcher was topping out at 96 mph on the radar gun.

Ritchie is now a member of the Atlanta Braves after being drafted 35th overall in the 2022 Major League Baseball draft.

Four years later, Kitsap County has another potential right-handed ace who attracted loads of NCAA Division I attention after reaching the low-to-mid 90s on his fastball this summer and fall: Kingston junior Vaka Tameilau.

Tameilau announced Tuesday, Nov. 17 his commitment to Vanderbilt University as a Class of 2028 recruit. The 16-year-old earned a full scholarship offer from the Commodores, who won the College World Series in 2014 and 2019.

"They're a great program, win a lot," Tameilau told the Kitsap Sun on Tuesday.

In addition to the full scholarship, Vanderbilt made a name, image and likeness (NIL) offer to secure Tameilau's commitment. He's keeping that number private for now, but it's significant.

Could Tameilau be on the same track as Ritchie, who committed to UCLA as a high schooler before his professional baseball prospects made him a high draft pick in 2022? Tameilau couldn't help but chuckle when he thought back on his younger days playing baseball, admitting he nearly gave up the sport.

"I almost quit. When I was 8, I was on the verge of quitting. My mom was like, 'No, you've got to do one more year, you've got to do one more year.'"

What was the reason Tameilau almost walked away from baseball?"Every time I got up to bat, I got hit over and over and over," he said. "I was like, 'I don't want to play anymore, Mom.'"

Tameilau is glad he listened to his mother, Jessica, and stayed with the sport. By the time he reached middle school, he was coming into his own as a pitcher. He nearly tossed a perfect game as a pre-teen in North Kitsap Little League, striking out 18 batters with the only baserunner being a hit batter.

Tameilau starting playing travel ball at age 12 and by the time he was a freshman in high school, his fastball was reaching the low 80s. As a sophomore at Kingston, Tameilau earned All-Olympic League honors as a pitcher. That spring, he was invited to join the Florida Travel Baseball (FTB) Phillies scout team, which competes in national showcase tournaments in places like Florida, Georgia and North Carolina.

For several months, Tameilau joined other Class of 2028 recruits from around the country in playing games that attract both college coaches and professional scouts. The scout team participation required a lot of cross-country air travel, but it proved to be worth it. Tameilau began eclipsing 90 mph regularly with his fastball and eventually topped out at 95.

"This summer, I think I did really well," Tameilau said.

College coaches shared the same opinion. Once the recruiting period opened in August, Tameilau was hit with a tidal wave of attention.

"Aug. 1 is the first day you can talk to people. It's like phone call after phone call after phone call," he said. "I think that first day, I took 25 calls. It's like speed dating 25 different people at the same time."

Tameilau narrowed down the list of interested schools and took six official visits, spending time at Oregon, Arizona State, Miami, Florida and Wake Forest in addition to Vanderbilt. In the end, Tameilau said he connected best with Commodores head coach Tim Corbin.

"That was the biggest part for me," he said. "I also wanted to go someplace warm."

It's not time for Tameilau to leave the Pacific Northwest just yet. Now that his college commitment is made, he's looking forward to playing on Kingston's basketball team this winter and getting back to a regular high school routine before baseball season rolls around next spring.

"I just want to keep everything normal. I just like being a high school kid, it's fun," he said. "I don't know if it's hit me yet how big of a deal it is. I know it's a huge deal and I'm super excited, but I still have a lot of time to go through high school and grow up."
